\chapter{RESULTS AND DISCUSSION}
\label{ch:results}

% =====================================================================
% Every table in this chapter is generated by code/make_tables.py from

% scripts. No cell is typed by hand. Re-running the pipeline updates the

\section{Introduction}

This chapter reports the experimental results. It first establishes the dataset
characterisation and calibration, then reports the three segmentation methods
under the leave-one-specimen-out protocol of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, then
tests the protocol itself against its naive alternative, and finally reports the
physical quantities the laboratory uses: bead count, areal density and the size
distribution in micrometres.

Two results are negative, and both are reported as prominently as the positive
ones. Mask R-CNN does not reach the provisional accuracy criterion set in
Section~\ref{sec:objectives}, and the naive partitioning protocol does not
overstate performance on this dataset in the way the literature on small
microscopy datasets would lead one to expect.

\section{Dataset Characterisation}

The descriptive analysis of the dataset is complete and is reported in
Chapter~\ref{ch:methodology}: 606 annotated beads across 11 micrographs of four
specimens, at three magnifications, with the pixel calibration of
Table~\ref{tab:calibration}.

The first objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met. The median equivalent
bead diameter is
7.92\,$\mu$m at $500\times$, 7.34\,$\mu$m at $1000\times$ and 6.75\,$\mu$m at
$3000\times$, an agreement of within 15\% against a stated criterion of 20\%. Since
the three magnifications image the same four specimens, this agreement is evidence
both that the scale calibration is correct and that the annotation is internally
consistent across magnifications -- an annotator who applied a different size
threshold at different magnifications would have broken it.

The residual downward trend with magnification is consistent with border clipping
rather than calibration error. At $3000\times$ the field is 94.8\,$\mu$m wide, so a
bead of 8\,$\mu$m occupies a much larger fraction of it and is correspondingly more
likely to intersect the image boundary and be excluded from annotation. Only 52 of
the 606 beads come from $3000\times$ micrographs, so this group is also the noisiest.

Pooled over all 11 micrographs and computed from rasterised masks rather than
polygon vertices, so as to be directly comparable with the predictions reported
later in this chapter, the manual median diameter is 7.97\,$\mu$m with an
interquartile range of 6.42 to 10.16\,$\mu$m.

\section{Experimental Setup}

\subsection{Training Configuration}

Table~\ref{tab:training_config} records the configuration used. Both models were
trained independently on each of the four folds from the same initialisation, on
a single NVIDIA T4.

\input{results/table_training_config}

\subsection{Justification of Training Hyperparameters}

Four settings depart from what a default configuration would give, and each was
chosen from a measured property of the data rather than by search. This matters
for how the results should be read: no hyperparameter was tuned against
performance, so none of them can have been fitted to the test partitions.

\textbf{Anchor sizes: 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 pixels.} The torchvision default
begins at 32 pixels. The median bead is 14 pixels across at $500\times$, so under
the default the majority of objects at the lowest magnification would have no
anchor within a factor of two of their size, and the region proposal network would
be asked to regress a large correction for most of the dataset. The chosen ladder
brackets the observed range of 14 to 76 pixels, widened at both ends to cover the
random scaling applied during training.

\textbf{Detection cap: 400 per image.} The COCO default is 100. Micrograph Z6-1
contains 152 annotated beads, so the default would have truncated its output
before any threshold was applied. The failure would have been silent and would
have biased exactly the quantity this work measures. The cap is set high enough
that it never binds.

\textbf{Crop size $512 \times 512$ with scale jitter from 0.5 to 2.0.} A
leave-one-specimen-out training partition holds eight micrographs. Training on
whole images would therefore present eight distinct inputs; random crops draw a
different field of view each time. The scaling range is wider than is usual
because scale robustness across a sixfold range in apparent object size is the
central difficulty of this dataset rather than an incidental nuisance.

\textbf{Score threshold: selected per fold on training data.} The threshold
applied to Mask R-CNN's output was chosen by maximising $F_1$ at an
intersection over union of 0.5 on each fold's own \emph{training} partition. The
selected values were 0.60, 0.70, 0.70 and 0.65 for folds Z2, Z4, Z5 and Z6. This
is the one free parameter of the learned pipeline, and selecting it on test data
would have inflated every number in this chapter. The U-Net's probability
threshold and minimum object area were chosen the same way, as were the three
parameters of the classical pipeline.

The number of training iterations, 1500, was set by the available GPU budget
rather than by a convergence criterion. This is a limitation and is recorded as
one in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}: the reported figures are what this
configuration produces, not what the architecture is capable of.

\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}

Every micrograph is scored exactly once, by the model of the fold that held its
specimen out. The eleven per-image results are therefore mutually independent in
the sense that no model contributed a score for a specimen it had seen, and
pooling them gives a single estimate over the whole dataset.

All three methods are evaluated by the same code, on the same predictions
format, against the same ground truth. This is not a convenience: a controlled
comparison is only meaningful if the differences between the methods come from the
methods. Each writes run-length-encoded masks in COCO results format, and the
evaluation module has no branch on which method produced them.

Metrics are computed at three levels, because a single number conceals the
failure modes that matter here. Average precision measures detection and
delineation jointly. The Aggregated Jaccard Index and Panoptic Quality measure
instance-level agreement, with Panoptic Quality decomposed into its recognition
and segmentation factors. Counting error, merge rate and split rate measure the
laboratory quantity directly. A method can score acceptably on the first and fail
completely on the third, and Section~\ref{sec:counting} shows that this is not a
hypothetical concern.

\subsection{Fold Composition}

\input{results/table_folds}

The folds are markedly unbalanced: specimen Z4 contributes only 63 beads across two
micrographs, while Z6 contributes 238 across three. Per-fold results are therefore
reported individually as well as averaged, since a mean over four folds of this
size is not a stable summary on its own.

\section{Segmentation Results}

\subsection{Mask R-CNN}

\input{results/table_maskrcnn_results}

Mask R-CNN reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.282 \pm 0.054$ averaged over the four
folds, with an Aggregated Jaccard Index of $0.315 \pm 0.036$ and a Panoptic
Quality of 0.352.

\textbf{This does not meet the provisional success criterion of
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} \geq 0.70$ stated in Section~\ref{sec:objectives}.} The third
objective is therefore not met at that threshold. The criterion was provisional
and awaits confirmation by the supervisor, but it is recorded here as stated
rather than adjusted after the fact to a value the result happens to clear.

The decomposition of Panoptic Quality is more informative than the headline
figure. Segmentation Quality -- the mean intersection over union of the beads
that were correctly matched -- is 0.720, while Recognition Quality is 0.487. The
model delineates well the beads it finds, and finds fewer than half of them. The
deficit is one of detection, not of boundary accuracy, and the gap between
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.282$ and $\mathrm{AP}_{75} = 0.069$ says the same thing from
the other direction: performance falls away sharply as the required overlap
tightens.

Per-fold results vary less than the counting results do. $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ ranges
from 0.232 on Z5 to 0.358 on Z2, and AJI from 0.273 on Z4 to 0.351 on Z6. Fold Z4
is the weakest on AJI and rests on only 63 beads across two micrographs, so it is
also the least reliable of the four.

\subsection{U-Net Semantic Baseline}

The U-Net baseline reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.152 \pm 0.042$, an AJI of 0.305
and a Panoptic Quality of 0.194. Its AJI is close to Mask R-CNN's, but its
Panoptic Quality is barely more than half, and the reason is visible in the
merge and split statistics.

The U-Net merges 48.7\% of ground-truth beads: nearly half of all annotated beads
end up inside a predicted region that has also swallowed at least one neighbour.
Its split rate is 0.0\%. It never fragments a bead and it very frequently fuses
adjacent ones, which is exactly the failure mode connected-component labelling
predicts. Two beads whose predicted regions touch by a single pixel become one
object, and no amount of semantic accuracy can undo that, because the information
distinguishing them was discarded when the instance identity was dropped.

The consequence for the measurement is direct: the U-Net under-counts by 44.2\%
on average, and the error is systematically signed. Every fold under-counts. A
method that merges cannot over-count, so its counting error carries a bias rather
than scatter, and no averaging over more micrographs will remove it.

This is the clearest quantitative answer to the question of what instance-level
modelling buys on this data. It is not primarily mask accuracy -- the two methods'
AJI values differ by only 0.010 -- but the ability to separate objects that touch.

\subsection{Classical Baseline}

The Otsu-plus-watershed pipeline fails on this data. It reaches
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$, an AJI of 0.067 and a Panoptic Quality of 0.013, and
over-counts by 574\% on average: 2205 objects reported against 606 annotated.

The failure has a measurable cause rather than being an artefact of poor tuning.
The contrast the method depends on is very weak: measured over the annotated
regions, the mean grey level inside a bead is 98 against 116 outside on Z2-1, 115
against 135 on Z5-2, and 81 against 104 on Z6-4 -- a separation of roughly 20 grey
levels in an image whose fibre network produces edges of comparable strength
everywhere. A global Otsu threshold therefore returns a speckled foreground whose
area bears little relation to the beads, and the distance-transform watershed then
partitions that speckle into hundreds of fragments.

Figure~\ref{fig:contrast} shows why no choice of threshold could have rescued the
method. The grey-level distributions inside and outside the beads are not merely
close; they overlap along almost their entire range. Any global threshold that
captured most bead pixels would also capture a large share of the background, and
one that excluded the background would exclude most of the beads. The failure is a
property of the images, not of the parameter search.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_contrast.pdf}
    \caption{Grey-level distributions inside and outside the annotated beads, for
    one micrograph at each magnification. The means differ by about 20 levels
    while the distributions overlap almost entirely, which is the condition under
    which global thresholding cannot work.}
    \label{fig:contrast}
\end{figure}

The parameters were tuned by grid search on each fold's training partition over
morphological kernel size, minimum accepted object area in $\mu$m$^2$ and marker
suppression distance. The grid brackets the median annotated bead area of about
38\,$\mu$m$^2$ from well below to well above, and the selected optimum falls in
the interior of the grid for all four folds, so the result is not an artefact of
too narrow a search.

Its Segmentation Quality of 0.489 against a Recognition Quality of 0.021 completes
the picture: on the rare occasion it matches a bead, the mask is not unreasonable;
it almost never matches one.

\subsection{Method Comparison}

\input{results/table_method_comparison}

The ranking is unambiguous and consistent across every metric: Mask R-CNN, then
the U-Net, then the classical pipeline. The fourth objective of
Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met.

The three methods fail in three different ways, and the counting column shows it
more clearly than the accuracy columns do. The classical pipeline over-counts by a
factor of seven because it fragments texture into objects. The U-Net under-counts
by 44\% because it fuses neighbours. Mask R-CNN's mean absolute counting error is
35.6\%, the lowest of the three, and it is the only method whose errors are not
systematically signed -- its mean signed error is $-2.9\%$, against $-44.2\%$ for
the U-Net and $+574.3\%$ for the classical pipeline.

That distinction matters for the application and is discussed further in
Section~\ref{sec:counting}, because a method whose errors cancel across specimens
is useful for a population estimate in a way that a biased method is not, while
still being unreliable for any single micrograph.

\subsection{Qualitative Examples}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_qualitative.pdf}
    \caption{The three methods on two held-out micrographs, Z6-1 at $500\times$
    and Z2-2 at $1000\times$. Every panel is produced by a model that never saw
    that specimen. Red outlines are the manual annotation, blue the prediction.}
    \label{fig:qualitative}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:qualitative} shows the three methods on two held-out micrographs,
and each of the numerical findings above has a visible counterpart in it.

On Z6-1 the annotator marked 152 beads. The classical pipeline returns 329
regions that tile the frame more or less irrespective of where the beads are:
its outlines follow the fibre texture, which is the visual form of an
$\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ of 0.001. The U-Net returns 77 regions, roughly half the true
count, and they are visibly larger than individual beads because adjacent beads
have been absorbed into single components --- the 48.7\% merge rate made visible.
Mask R-CNN returns 120 regions that correspond recognisably to individual beads,
and its errors are of a different kind: beads missed entirely rather than beads
fused together.

On Z2-2, where the annotator marked 51 beads, the same pattern holds at a
different scale. The classical pipeline returns 311 regions; the U-Net 31 and
Mask R-CNN 37, both under-counting, but the U-Net's regions again span
neighbouring beads while Mask R-CNN's do not.

The panels also show what the summary statistics cannot: the beads themselves are
low-contrast objects embedded in a dense fibre network, and in several places the
distinction between a bead and a locally thickened fibre crossing is genuinely
ambiguous to the eye. This is the limitation recorded in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations} concerning the single annotation class, and it
places an unknown ceiling on what any model can be expected to achieve against
this ground truth.

\section{The Cost of a Naive Split}
\label{sec:leakage}

\input{results/table_leakage}

This is a negative result and it is reported as measured.

Evaluating the same model under a random split over the 11 micrographs, with fold
sizes identical to the specimen-wise protocol, gives
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.284$ against 0.282 for leave-one-specimen-out -- a
difference of 0.0029, against a between-fold standard deviation of 0.054 for the
specimen-wise protocol. AJI differs by 0.0014 and mean absolute counting error by
0.5 percentage points. On this dataset, the naive protocol does not overstate
performance.

The second objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} asked for a demonstration
that the naive alternative overstates performance, and that demonstration did not
materialise. The protocol remains the correct one to use, but on the strength of
structural argument rather than of measured inflation, and the distinction should
be stated rather than blurred.

Three factors plausibly explain the absence of a gap, and the first is the most
likely.

\textbf{The leak that mattered had already been removed.} The 132 pre-computed
augmented copies were discarded before any partitioning, as described in
Section~\ref{sec:supplied_aug}. Those copies are near-duplicates of their
originals, and allowing them to cross a partition boundary would put a
transformed version of a test image directly into training. The remaining
dependence between two micrographs of the same specimen at different
magnifications is far weaker: they show different fields of view at different
scales, and share only the specimen's general morphology.

\textbf{There is little headroom to inflate.} A protocol can only flatter a model
that is capable of memorising. At $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.28$ and a Recognition
Quality of 0.49, this model is under-fitting the task rather than memorising
specimens, and there is correspondingly little for a leak to exploit.

\textbf{With 11 images, both protocols are noisy.} The random split's folds range
from $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.160$ to 0.417, a spread of 0.257, against 0.232 to
0.358 for the specimen-wise folds, a spread of 0.126. The random protocol did not
give a higher mean, but it gave one that varies twice as much between folds. That
is a reason to prefer the specimen-wise protocol independent of any bias
argument: it is the more stable estimator, and on four folds stability is worth
more than it would be on forty.

The honest conclusion is that on this dataset the choice of protocol changes the
answer very little, and that the argument for partitioning by specimen rests on
what could happen with a stronger model and on estimator variance, not on a
measured gap in these runs.

\section{Behaviour Across Magnification}
\label{sec:magnification}

\input{results/table_magnification}

Performance improves monotonically with magnification, which is the opposite of
what the sample sizes alone would predict. The $3000\times$ group is the smallest
in the dataset -- 52 beads across four micrographs, against 325 at $500\times$ --
and it is nonetheless the group on which the model performs best, at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.369$ and AJI 0.367 against 0.234 and 0.255 at $500\times$.

Object size, not sample size, is the binding constraint. The median bead is 14
pixels across at $500\times$ and 76 at $3000\times$. At 14 pixels a bead spans
roughly the receptive field of the finest pyramid level and is only a few pixels
larger than the smallest anchor, and the boundary of such an object is decided by
a handful of pixels; at 76 pixels it is a comfortably resolved object. The
feature pyramid and the rescaled anchors were introduced to handle this sixfold
range, and Table~\ref{tab:magnification} shows that they narrow the gap without
closing it.

This has a practical consequence for the laboratory, which is the reverse of the
usual advice. If bead quantification is the goal, imaging at higher magnification
gives more reliable per-bead measurements, at the cost of a smaller field and
therefore a noisier estimate of areal density. The $1000\times$ setting is the
worst of both on this evidence: its counting error is the highest of the three at
45.2\%.

The caveat is that 52 beads is a small sample, and the $3000\times$ figures should
be read as indicative rather than settled.

\section{Physical Quantification}

\subsection{Bead Count and Areal Density}
\label{sec:counting}

Summed over all 11 held-out micrographs, Mask R-CNN reports 543 beads against 606
annotated, an aggregate shortfall of 10.4\%. That figure is more favourable than
the method deserves, because it is the sum of errors that largely cancel.

Per specimen the signed error runs from $-32.0\%$ on Z4 to $+45.5\%$ on Z6, and
per micrograph from $-67.6\%$ on Z5-1 to $+95.2\%$ on Z6-2. The mean absolute
error per fold is 35.6\% while the mean signed error is $-2.9\%$. A single
micrograph is therefore not a reliable measurement, and an aggregate over many
micrographs is considerably better than any one of them.

Figure~\ref{fig:counting} plots the two counts against each other. Six of the
eleven micrographs fall within 25\% of the annotated count, but the two outliers
are large and lie on opposite sides: Z5-1 is under-counted by two thirds, and
Z6-2 is nearly doubled. Both are among the more densely populated micrographs,
which is where a merge or a spurious split costs most.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.78\textwidth]{figures/fig_counting.pdf}
    \caption{Predicted against annotated bead count for each held-out micrograph,
    with marker shape indicating magnification. Points on the diagonal agree
    exactly. The aggregate shortfall of 10.4\% is the net effect of errors that
    run in both directions and largely cancel.}
    \label{fig:counting}
\end{figure}

Areal density inherits this behaviour directly, since it is the count divided by a
known physical area. On Z2-1 the model reports 348 beads\,mm$^{-2}$ against 305
measured manually; on Z5-1 it reports 142 against 438; on Z6-2, 2080 against 1066.
The fifth objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met in the sense that these
quantities are reported and compared, but the comparison does not support using
the pipeline as a drop-in replacement for manual counting on a single field.

\subsection{Size Distribution Agreement}

\input{results/table_physical}

Mask R-CNN's predicted median diameter is 7.70\,$\mu$m against 7.97\,$\mu$m
measured manually, a difference of 3.4\%, with an interquartile range of 5.75 to
9.12\,$\mu$m against 6.42 to 10.16\,$\mu$m. The predicted distribution is
slightly narrower and slightly smaller, consistent with a detector that misses
the beads hardest to delineate and trims the boundaries of those it keeps.

All three two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests reject the hypothesis that the
predicted and manual distributions are the same, at $p < 10^{-3}$. That
rejection should not be over-read. With 543 and 606 samples the test is sensitive
to differences far smaller than those that would matter for process
optimisation, and statistical significance here is not the same as practical
disagreement: a 3.4\% error in median bead diameter is smaller than the 15\%
spread the same annotation shows across magnifications.

Figure~\ref{fig:size_agreement} shows why the summary statistics should be read
alongside the distributions. Mask R-CNN tracks the manual distribution closely
through its bulk and falls short in the tail above roughly 15\,$\mu$m.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{figures/fig_size_agreement.pdf}
    \caption{Predicted against manual bead size distributions, pooled over all
    11 held-out micrographs.}
    \label{fig:size_agreement}
\end{figure}

One result in Table~\ref{tab:physical} is a warning rather than a finding. The
classical pipeline has the \emph{lowest} Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistic of the
three methods, $D = 0.105$, while being by every other measure the worst method
by a wide margin. It achieves this by reporting 2205 objects whose sizes happen to
span a similar range to the real beads. Distributional agreement alone is
therefore not a sufficient criterion: a method can reproduce the size distribution
of a population it has almost entirely failed to identify, and this is exactly why
counting error and instance-level metrics are reported alongside it rather than
in its place.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Key Findings}

\textbf{Instance segmentation is the right formulation, and the reason is
separation rather than accuracy.} Mask R-CNN and the U-Net differ by 0.010 in
AJI but by 0.158 in Panoptic Quality and by 26.6 percentage points in merge rate.
What the instance formulation buys on this data is the ability to keep touching
beads apart. That the annotation itself contains 8.8\% overlapping bead pixels
confirms that touching beads are common rather than exceptional here.

\textbf{Classical thresholding is not a viable baseline for this modality.} At
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$ it is not merely worse than the learned methods but
unusable, and the measured bead-to-background separation of about 20 grey levels
explains why.

\textbf{The absolute performance is not yet sufficient for unattended use.} An
$\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ of 0.282 and a per-fold counting error of 35.6\% do not support
replacing a human operator. What the pipeline can support is triage and
aggregate estimation.

\textbf{Small objects, not scarce labels, are the binding constraint.} Performance
is best where the data are scarcest and the objects are largest.

\textbf{The specimen-wise protocol did not change the headline number, but it
halved the variance.} That is a weaker claim than the one anticipated in
Section~\ref{sec:objectives}, and it is the one the data support.

\subsection{Comparison with the Literature}

Direct numerical comparison with published work is not possible, because no public
benchmark for bead defects in electrospun mats exists and the AP values reported
here are specific to this annotation and this protocol. Three qualitative
comparisons can be made.

The merge behaviour of semantic segmentation with connected-component
post-processing is well documented in the nuclei segmentation literature, and is
the motivation for the boundary-aware and shape-prior methods of
Schmidt et al.\ \cite{schmidt2018stardist} and Stringer et al.\
\cite{stringer2021cellpose} and for the weighted-boundary loss of the original
U-Net \cite{ronneberger2015unet, falk2019unet}. The 48.7\% merge rate measured
here is a direct instance of that effect, and its magnitude is a consequence of
how frequently beads touch in these micrographs.

The difficulty of small objects for region-based detectors is likewise a known
property of the architecture rather than of this dataset, and is what the feature
pyramid \cite{lin2017feature} was introduced to address. The result of
Table~\ref{tab:magnification} is consistent with the general finding that
performance degrades with object size in pixels.

The absolute values reported here are well below those typically reported on
nuclei benchmarks such as the dataset of Kumar et al.\ \cite{kumar2017dataset}.
The relevant difference is training set size: those results rest on tens of
thousands of annotated objects, against 606 here from four specimens, of which
roughly three-quarters are available for training in any fold.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The limitations below follow from the dataset and from the experimental design.

\textbf{Four specimens.} The strongest claim this dataset can support is
generalisation across four specimens of what appears to be one material system. It
cannot establish generalisation to a different polymer, a different solvent or a
different instrument.

\textbf{Fifty-two beads at $3000\times$.} The highest magnification is represented by
only 52 annotated objects, so the per-magnification result for $3000\times$ --
which is also the most striking finding of
Section~\ref{sec:magnification} -- rests on a small sample
and should be read as indicative.

\textbf{One annotator.} All 606 annotations come from a single source, so
annotator bias cannot be distinguished from ground truth, and no inter-annotator
agreement can be reported. This matters more than usual here, because at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.282$ it is not known how much of the shortfall is model
error and how much is disagreement that a second annotator would also show.
% TODO(supervisor): if a subset can be re-annotated by a second person, this
% limitation can be converted into a measurement instead. See question D4.

\textbf{Single class.} The annotation does not distinguish beads from locally
thickened fibre segments, so the boundary between the two is defined implicitly by
the annotator's judgement rather than by a stated criterion. Several of the
model's false positives on visual inspection are objects of this ambiguous kind.

\textbf{No hyperparameter search.} Every model was trained once, with the
configuration of Table~\ref{tab:training_config}, for 1500 iterations. The
reported figures are what that configuration produces, not the best achievable,
and the training budget was set by the available GPU time rather than by
convergence.

\subsection{Reliability of the Reported Numbers}

Each configuration was run \emph{once}, with a fixed seed of 0. No seed was
varied and no configuration was repeated, so every figure in this chapter is a
single-run point estimate and none of the reported standard deviations is a
measure of run-to-run variability. They are between-fold spreads over four folds,
which is a different and weaker quantity: it describes how much the result
depends on which specimen was held out, not how much it would move if the same
experiment were repeated.

With four folds, a standard deviation is itself estimated from four numbers and
should not be treated as a confidence interval. Varoquaux
\cite{varoquaux2018crossvalidation} shows that cross-validated estimates from small
samples carry error bars far wider than is usually assumed, and that differences
well below those error bars are routinely reported as findings. The comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:leakage} is the one most exposed to this: a difference of 0.0029
between protocols is far below the resolution these runs can distinguish, so the
correct reading is that no difference was detected, not that the two protocols
were shown to be equivalent.

What can be stated robustly is the ranking of the three methods, which is
consistent across every metric and every fold, and the direction of the merge and
counting biases, which are large and systematically signed. What cannot be stated
robustly is any small difference between two similar numbers.

\section{Summary}

Mask R-CNN outperforms both baselines on every metric measured, reaching
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.282 \pm 0.054$, AJI $0.315 \pm 0.036$ and a mean absolute
counting error of 35.6\% under leave-one-specimen-out cross-validation. It does
not reach the provisional criterion of $\mathrm{AP}_{50} \geq 0.70$.

The U-Net baseline merges 48.7\% of beads and under-counts by 44\%, which
identifies object separation rather than mask accuracy as what the instance
formulation contributes. The classical pipeline fails outright, at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$, for a reason measurable in the images themselves.

Performance improves with magnification despite the smallest sample being at the
highest magnification, identifying object size in pixels as the binding
constraint. The naive partitioning protocol did not overstate performance,
though it produced fold-to-fold variance twice as large. Predicted bead diameters
agree with the manual measurement to 3.4\% in the median, while counting remains
too variable per micrograph for unattended use.
